text:
# The Lighthouse Keeper's Ledger

The ledger was found in a tin box under the floorboards of the keeper's cottage at Carrow Point, three years after the light was automated and the last man went ashore for good. It was bound in green cloth gone black at the corners. Its first entry was dated the fourth of March, and the year had been scratched out, deliberately, so hard the nib went through the paper.

What follows is the ledger, more or less, along with what came after.

---

**4 March.** Wind SW, force 6. Barometer falling. Lamp lit 18:12. Wicks trimmed twice. A gull struck the gallery glass at 21:40 and did not survive. I buried it in the rocks below the oil store, which I suppose is foolish. Davies would have laughed. Davies is gone now, though, and the laughing with him, so I bury what I like.

**5 March.** Wind SW backing S, force 7. Rain. Lamp lit 18:14. No vessels sighted. The supply boat is due Thursday if the sea allows, which it will not.

**6 March.** Wind S, force 8. Heavy seas over the landing. I did not go down. Lamp lit 18:15. At some hour past midnight I heard knocking at the lower door. Went down with the lantern. Nobody. The sea had thrown a plank against it, I expect. There was no plank when I looked.

**7 March.** Wind S, force 7, easing. I have decided to write more in this book than the Board requires. The Board requires weather, lamp, vessels, stores. The Board does not require me to say that I am lonely. But the Board will never read this book, because I have bought it myself in Penmorran for one and six, and the Board's book is the other one, the blue one, which I keep in proper order on the desk downstairs. This one is mine.

---

I should explain how I came to have it.

My name doesn't matter much to the story, but it's Ilse Treharne, and I was sent to Carrow Point by the heritage trust to survey the cottage before it was converted into holiday lets. That's what happens to lighthouses now. The lamps run themselves, monitored from an office in Harwich, and the cottages where men once lived in shifts of eight weeks become places where couples from Bristol spend long weekends and leave reviews about the water pressure.

I'm not sentimental about this. I want that on the record. I am a surveyor; I measure damp and count joists and write reports about lintels. I was on my hands and knees in the back bedroom because the floor had a soft spot near the window, and when I lifted the board to check for rot, there was the tin.

I opened it. Of course I did. Anyone would.

---

**9 March.** Wind W, force 4. Clear. The supply boat came after all. Pengelly brought paraffin, flour, tea, a side of bacon, three tins of peaches, letters. One letter for me, from my sister in Truro. She asks if I am eating. She asks if the nights are long. She says Mother has been asking for me again, by name, which she has not done since Christmas.

I asked Pengelly whether a relief keeper has been found to replace Davies. He said the Board is "looking into it," and then he looked at the sea and not at me, which is how men look when they know a thing and won't say it.

**10 March.** Wind W, force 3. Fine. I have been thinking about the knocking. I am not a fanciful man. I was eleven years at the Wolf Rock and four at Longships and I never once heard a thing I could not account for. But Davies told me, the first week I came here, that Carrow had "a guest." That was the word. Not a ghost. A guest. I asked him what he meant and he said, "You'll know if it comes. Be civil." I took it for the sort of thing old keepers say to new ones, like telling an apprentice to fetch a tin of tartan paint.

Davies has been dead six weeks. He went off the gallery in the January gale. They say he slipped. I found him on the rocks in the morning and I did not think he had slipped, though I said nothing, because what would I say.

---

I read that entry standing in the empty bedroom with the late light coming flat across the bay, and I felt the particular unease you get when a document turns out to be more than a document. I put the book back in its tin. I finished my survey — the soft spot was rot, as I'd thought, wet rot from a failed downpipe outside — and I drove back to the B&B in Penmorran with the tin on the passenger seat like a passenger.

The landlady, Mrs. Ogunleye, had married into the village thirty years ago and knew everything about it, the way incomers often do — better than the people born there, who never had to learn. I asked her about Carrow Point over a plate of something she called a "proper tea," which turned out to be a whole roast dinner.

"The lighthouse? Oh, they've all got stories," she said. "Every light on this coast has a story. Men out there on their own, what do you expect."

"Do you know of a keeper called Davies? Died in a fall?"

She considered. "There's a Davies in the churchyard, up by the wall. I don't know if he was a keeper. There's a lot of Davieses."

---

**12 March.** Wind NW, force 5. Squalls. Lamp lit 18:20. A steamer passed at 22:00 bound north, showing proper lights. I signalled and she answered. It is a comfort to be answered.

**13 March.** Wind NW, force 4. I have been through Davies's things, which the Board has not yet sent for. Not much. Clothes, a razor, a Bible with nothing written in it, a tobacco tin with seven shillings in it, a photograph of a woman standing in a doorway. On the back of the photograph: *Carrow, 18—*, and again the year scratched out. The doorway in the photograph is the doorway of this cottage. I would know it anywhere; the step has the same crack.

I do not know who the woman is. Davies never mentioned a wife. Keepers' wives lived ashore by then; the Board did not permit families on the rock after the Gwennap affair.

**14 March.** Calm. Fog. Fog signal operated from 04:00 to 11:30. A long morning of it. When the fog lifted I went down to the landing and found, laid on the top step, a row of seven pebbles, white ones, the kind you find in the cove at Porthallow and not here. Here the stones are black.

I left them where they were. Be civil, Davies said.

---

That night in the B&B I didn't sleep well. I kept thinking about the pebbles. I'm aware of how that sounds. I lay there listening to the sea, which you can hear from everywhere in Penmorran, the whole village built in a fold of the cliff like something tucked into a pocket, and I thought: seven pebbles, seven shillings.

It means nothing. Coincidences are cheap; the world produces them at industrial volume. I know that.

In the morning I went to the churchyard.

---

The Davies by the wall was Thomas Davies, "Keeper of the Carrow Light," died January, year weathered to illegibility. Beneath the name, smaller: *And Mary his wife, who waited.*

Who waited.

I stood there for a long time. A man came along the path with a strimmer and a flask, nodded to me, and began work on the far end of the yard, the noise ripping through the morning. I took a photograph of the stone on my phone and then, feeling oddly guilty, as though I'd stolen something, I put the phone away.

---

**16 March.** Wind E, force 3. Bright and cold. I have read Davies's Bible after all. Not for the scripture; I was looking for anything. In the back, under the endpaper, which had come unglued, there is a letter. I copy it here because I mean to burn the original. It is not a thing that should be left.

> *Tom —*
>
> *I know you said not to come but I will come anyway on the Thursday boat if Pengelly will take me. I cannot keep on in Truro with your mother looking at me that way. I would rather be out there with you and the wind than in that house with her. If the Board finds out let them. What can they do, take the light away? They cannot take the light away, Tom, it is the only thing that is ours.*
>
> *I will bring the white stones from Porthallow like you asked. One for each year. Seven years Tom. Seven years since the church and I have spent maybe one in all of it with you.*
>
> *Your Mary.*

I have not burned it. I have put it back in the Bible and put the Bible in Davies's sea chest and closed the lid. I find I cannot do it.

**17 March.** Wind E, force 4. Lamp lit 18:25. I asked Pengelly when he came — he came today, unexpected, with a part for the clockwork — whether he had ever taken a woman out to Carrow. He went very quiet. Then he said, "Once." Then he said, "She never came back on my boat." Then he said he had to catch the tide and he was gone before I could ask him anything else, and the part for the clockwork was the wrong part.

---

I want to stop here and say something about the work of reading old documents, because I've done a fair amount of it for my job — tithe maps, sale particulars, the letters people tuck behind skirting boards. There's a temptation, when you find something like this ledger, to make it into a story. To assume it's leading somewhere, that it has a shape, that the shape is meaningful. Most of the time, the real past doesn't have a shape. It has a lot of weather and a lot of stores and the occasional gull against the glass. People lived, and then they stopped, and in between they bought paraffin and complained about the Board.

But I'm also a person who reads, and I know that sometimes the shape is real. Sometimes a man sits at a desk at the end of the world and writes down the truth because there's nobody to tell it to.

I kept reading.

---

**19 March.** Wind SE, force 6. I have been lying to myself, and this book was meant to be the place where I do not do that, so I will set it down.

I knew about Mary. Not her name — Davies never said her name — but I knew there had been a woman. The first week I was here, I found a hairpin in the crack between the floorboards in the back bedroom. A plain black hairpin. I asked Davies about it and he took it from my hand and put it in his pocket and said, "Leave it, boy," though I am forty-one and he was not much older.

And I knew, though I told nobody, that on the night Davies went off the gallery, he was not alone up there. I was in my bunk, off watch, and I heard him talking. I thought he was talking to himself, as keepers do. But I heard him stop, as though listening, and then answer. And then he laughed, the way a man laughs when he is happy, which I had never heard him do. And then nothing. And in the morning he was on the rocks.

I told the inquiry he slipped. I did not tell them he was laughing.

**20 March.** Calm. I sat on the gallery last night after the lamp was lit, wrapped in the oilskin, and I said aloud, "Mary." I don't know why. To see. Nothing happened. The light went round. The sea breathed. After a while I felt very foolish and went in.

But this morning, on my pillow, there was a hairpin.

---

That was where I stopped reading, the second night, because the next page was stuck to the one after it with something I didn't want to think about too closely, probably damp, possibly not damp. I didn't want to tear it. I'm a professional. You don't tear the page.

I called my brother instead. Kit lives in Leeds and teaches chemistry at a sixth-form college and has a policy of answering the phone on the first ring no matter what, a policy he adopted after our father died and he missed the call.

"You found a haunted diary," he said.

"I found a ledger. It's a keeper's ledger."

"With a ghost in it."

"With a man in it who thinks there's a ghost in it. That's different."

"Is it?" said Kit, who, despite being a chemist, has always been the one in the family who believes things. He believes in acupuncture and in the healing properties of certain brands of honey and, I'm fairly sure, in God, though we don't talk about that. "Ilse. What are you going to do with it?"

"Hand it to the trust. It's their property, technically. It was found on their site."

"Are you, though?"

I didn't answer. Out the window, the beam from Carrow came round over the bay, steady, every fifteen seconds, the way it had for a hundred and sixty years. Automated now. Nobody trimming the wicks. Nobody on the gallery.

"I want to know how it ends," I said.

"Then find out," said Kit. "And then decide."

---

In the morning I took the ledger to the county records office in Truro, because they have a conservator there, a woman named Priya Venkataraman who I'd worked with before on a bundle of eighteenth-century leases found in a chimney. She looked at the stuck pages and made a small noise of professional delight and said she could separate them in about a week.

"Can't you do it faster?"

"I could do it faster and destroy it," she said. "Or I could do it in a week and not."

So I had a week. I spent it doing what I actually know how to do, which is research.

---

The Trinity House records — Carrow was a Trinity House light, though the ledger's author keeps calling his employers "the Board," which I think was just a keeper's shorthand — are partly digitised and partly not. The partly-not was in a reading room in London that I didn't have time to visit. The partly-digitised gave me this:

Thomas Davies, Principal Keeper, Carrow Point. Appointed in a year I won't specify, because the ledger's author clearly didn't want it specified and I've come, absurdly, to feel some loyalty to him. Died on station, January, cause of death recorded as "accidental fall from gallery during gale."

Assistant Keeper at the time of death: Samuel Hosking.

Samuel Hosking. That was him, then. The man writing the ledger. The man who buried a gull in the rocks.

Samuel Hosking remained at Carrow Point for — and here I sat back in my chair in the B&B's little conservatory, with Mrs. Ogunleye's cat asleep on the radiator — for thirty-one more years. He never transferred. He was offered promotion to Principal at Longships, twice, and declined both times. He retired at seventy, which was past the usual age, and he died the same year, in Penmorran, in a room above what is now the post office.

Thirty-one years on that rock, by choice.

---

Mrs. Ogunleye, when I told her this, said, "Hosking? There's still Hoskings in the village. There's a Ruth Hosking up at Chapel Row, she must be ninety. You could ask her."

So I did.

---

Ruth Hosking was ninety-three and sharp as a bradawl. She lived in a cottage that smelled of coal tar soap and had, on every flat surface, a photograph or a shell or a small brass object that had been polished to the point of featurelessness. She received me in an armchair with a blanket over her knees and a look on her face that said she'd been expecting someone to come about this for a long time.

"Samuel was my great-uncle," she said. "Grandfather's brother. I knew him when I was a little girl. He used to come for Sunday dinner when he was ashore. Tall man. Very quiet. Smelled of paraffin, always. Even after he retired, Mother said, the smell never came off him."

"Did he ever talk about Carrow?"

"Not to children." She looked at me. "You've found something."

I told her. I hadn't intended to tell her everything, but I did — the ledger, Davies, Mary, the pebbles, the hairpin. She listened without interrupting. When I finished she was quiet for a while, looking past me at the window, where a grey gull had settled on the sill outside and was regarding us both with an expression of total contempt.

"Mother told me a thing once," she said at last. "When I was grown. She said Uncle Samuel never married because he said he was 'already spoken for.' That's how he put it. Already spoken for. The family thought he meant the light. That he was married to the light, you know, the way they say priests are married to the church." She turned her head and looked at me directly. "But Mother didn't think that's what he meant."

"What did she think?"

"She thought there was a woman." Ruth smiled, very slightly. "She thought it was a woman nobody could see."

---

I went back to the B&B and lay on the bed and looked at the ceiling. There was a water stain shaped roughly like Ireland. Professional habit made me assess it: failed flashing on the dormer, probably, intermittent, not urgent. I thought about Samuel Hosking, forty-one years old, writing *I find I cannot do it* about a letter that wasn't his. I thought about him sitting on the gallery saying a dead woman's name into the wind to see what would happen.

I thought: thirty-one years.

I'm thirty-eight. I've been alone, in the specific sense of the word, for about four of those years, since Josh and I split up — amicably, as these things go, which is to say we were both relieved and both sad and both too tired to fight about the furniture. I have friends. I have Kit. I have my work, which I'm good at and which takes me to strange old buildings full of other people's leftover lives. I'm not unhappy.

But I lay there and thought about what it would mean to choose a haunted rock over everything else, for thirty-one years, and I found I didn't think it was madness. I thought it might be the opposite. I thought it might be a man who found the one thing that was his — *they cannot take the light away, Tom, it is the only thing that is ours* — and decided to keep it.

---

Priya called on the sixth day.

"It's done," she said. "The pages are separated. There's — " She paused. "There's quite a lot more. He wrote very small, at the end. And there's something stuck between the last two pages. You'll want to see it."

---

**22 March.** I have not slept two nights together. Not from fear. I want to be plain about that, in case anyone does read this. I am not afraid. I am something I don't have a word for.

She is here. Or something is here. I hear her on the stair — light, quicker than a man's tread. I smell, sometimes, lavender water, which there is none of in the station. I find the kettle warm when I have not boiled it. Last night I came down from the watch at 02:00 and the table was laid. One cup, one plate. The good plate, the blue one Davies kept on the high shelf.

I sat down and I ate the bread that was on it, which was bread I had baked myself on Tuesday, and I said thank you. Be civil.

**23 March.** I have worked it out, I think, or some of it. She came out on Pengelly's boat to be with Davies, against the rules. Seven years married and hardly a year together. She meant to stay hidden, I suppose, in the back bedroom, until the Board found out or didn't. And something happened to her here. I don't know what. Whether she fell, or took ill, or — I don't know. But she never left. Pengelly never took her back. And Davies, who had loved her enough to ask for seven white stones, one for each year, kept her secret and kept the light, alone with her, until the night in January when he went up on the gallery and laughed and stepped off.

I don't think he slipped. I think she called him and he went.

And now he is gone where she could not follow, perhaps. Or perhaps they are together and she is here only as an echo, the way the bell keeps sounding in your ears after the fog signal stops. I don't know how these things work. Nobody does.

But she lays the table. She leaves the pebbles. She puts the hairpin on my pillow.

I think she is lonely too.

**24 March.** Wind W, force 3. Lamp lit 18:31. I have written to the Board to say I do not require a relief keeper and will manage the station alone until further notice. This is against regulations. They will say no. Let them.

**28 March.** The Board says no. A relief keeper, Jago, is to come out on the first of April. A young man from St Ives. He will have the back bedroom.

**29 March.** I told her. I sat on the gallery and I told her, out loud, that a young man was coming, and that he was not to be frightened, and that she was not to — I did not know how to finish the sentence. Not to call him. Not to do what she did to Davies, if she did it.

The wind dropped completely. Dead calm. The sea went flat as a plate. I have never known it so still at Carrow, never, not in all the months. And then, very close to my ear, close enough that I felt it on my skin, someone said, *I would never.*

Just that.

I believed her.

**1 April.** Jago arrived. He is nineteen and talks a great deal and is afraid of the dark, which he hides badly. I gave him my room and took the back bedroom myself. He asked why. I told him the back room was warmer. He did not argue.

---

There followed, Priya told me as she laid the pages out on the conservation table under the lamp, about twenty years of entries. Twenty years of weather. Lamp lit, lamp extinguished. Vessels. Stores. Jago came and went; other assistants came and went. The steamers gave way to motor vessels. Pengelly died and his son took over the boat. Hosking's handwriting changed over the decades, grew larger and then smaller, the confident copperplate of a man in his forties becoming the cramped, careful script of a man in his sixties who knows his eyes are going and does not want to waste paper.

And, threaded through it, rarely — once in a season, sometimes less — a single line.

*Table laid.*

*Lavender.*

*She sat with me on the gallery tonight. The light went round.*

*Pebbles on the step — eight. She is counting something. I do not know what.*

*Nine.*

*She hummed. I knew the tune; it was "The White Rose." My mother sang it.*

*Pebbles — fourteen.*

*Twenty.*

---

"The last entries," said Priya, "are the ones I wanted you to see."

---

**3 October.** Wind NW, force 5. Lamp lit 17:58. This is my last watch at Carrow. Tomorrow the boat comes and I go ashore for good. Seventy years old and they will not keep me longer, and I suppose they are right. My hands shake now trimming the wicks. Young Polglase does it better than I do, though I would not tell him so.

I have been thirty-one years at this station. I have kept this book for all of them, though there are gaps — whole years I could not bring myself to write in it, and years when I wrote nothing but weather because the weather was all there was.

I want to write down the truth before I go. Whoever finds this, if anyone does:

I was not unhappy here. I want that understood. People in the village think I was strange, and perhaps I was. They think I was hiding from something, or punishing myself, or that I was "a bit soft," as Pengelly's boy once said when he thought I could not hear. None of that is so.

I stayed because I was keeping a light, and because I was keeping someone company who had nobody else. Davies left her. I do not blame him — I think he could not bear it, being so close and not close enough — but he left her. And she was civil to me when I was civil to her, and over thirty years that civility became something I can only call friendship, and then something past friendship that I have no name for and will not try to name now.

I never saw her face. I want that understood too. Not once in thirty-one years. I heard her and I smelled her and once — once — on a night in the winter of the big freeze, I woke with a hand resting on my forehead, cool and light, like a mother's hand on a sick child, and I lay very still and did not open my eyes for fear she would take it away. She did not take it away. In the morning it was gone and I had slept better than I had in years.

That is what I have to show for my life. A hand on my forehead, once. The table laid. A tune hummed on the gallery. Pebbles on the step.

It is more than a great many men get. I know that now.

**4 October.** Calm. Clear. Sunrise 07:22. Lamp extinguished 07:30, last time by my hand.

I went down to the landing in the half-light to look at the sea one more time before the boat. On the top step there were thirty-one white pebbles, in a row, very straight.

One for each year.

She was counting. She was counting my years the way Mary counted hers with Davies. Seven years married, and not one of them together. Thirty-one years with me, and every one of them together, after a fashion.

I picked them up. All of them. I have them in my coat pocket as I write this. I mean to take them ashore.

I went back up to the gallery and I said — I said the name. Not Mary. I had stopped calling her Mary years ago; it did not seem right, it was Davies's name for her and she was not Davies's anymore. I had another name for her that I will not write down. It is the only thing I will keep back from this book.

I said it, and I said goodbye, and I said thank you.

And the light came round — I had extinguished it, there was no light, the lamp was cold, I swear on my life it was cold — the light came round, once, and went over me, and over the sea, and was gone.

Boat's in. Polglase is calling up the stair. I am going to put this book under the floor of the back bedroom, where she will know where it is.

God keep you, my dear. Keep the light.

*S.H.*

---

Between the last two pages, flattened by more than a century, was a small white stone. Not a pebble from the cove at Porthallow — I learned later that the Porthallow stones are quartz, and this was quartz too, but older, rounder, worn to a near-perfect sphere. It had been wrapped in a scrap of paper on which was written, in a hand that was not Samuel Hosking's — a rounder hand, quicker, a woman's hand, I would have said, though I know you can't really tell — a single word.

*Kept.*

---

I didn't hand the ledger to the trust.

I want to be honest about that, the way Samuel Hosking was honest in his book. It was technically their property. I technically had a professional obligation. I wrote, instead, in my survey report, that the rot in the back bedroom had been remediated "with original materials retained in situ where possible." Which is true, in its way.

What I did was this. I went back to Carrow Point at the end of October, after the work was signed off but before the first holiday guests arrived. The contractor had finished the back bedroom. New joists, same boards, sanded and sealed. I had a key.

I lifted the board. I put the tin back underneath it, with the ledger inside, and the white stone, and a note of my own that I'm not going to reproduce here because it was mine. I put the board down and screwed it back into place, and I made sure the screws were countersunk properly, because I'm a surveyor and I can't help it.

Then I climbed the tower.

The lantern room at Carrow is all brass and glass, the great Fresnel lens still in place though the lamp inside it is now a small LED cluster no bigger than a fist. It turns on a motor that hums. The gallery outside runs all the way round, with an iron rail at about hip height, the rail Thomas Davies went over in a January gale a hundred and sixty-odd years ago, laughing.

It was dusk. The lamp came on automatically while I stood there. It went round. Every fifteen seconds, steady, the way it always had.

I said — I don't know what I expected — I said, "Hello." And then, feeling ridiculous: "I put the book back. It's where you left it. Where he left it. I thought you'd want it."

Nothing. The sea. The hum of the motor. A cormorant going home low over the water.

I waited a long time. Long enough for the cold to come up through my boots. And I'll tell you what happened, and you can make of it what you like. I've told Kit and he believes me, and I've told Priya and she doesn't, and I've told Ruth Hosking, who died in the spring at ninety-four and who held my hand when I told her and said, "Good. Good. Oh, good."

What happened was nothing visible. Nothing I could put in a report. But the wind, which had been blowing steady from the south-west all day, force 4 or 5 — I'd checked the forecast, it's habit — the wind dropped. All at once. Dead calm. And the sea below the rocks went flat and still as a plate, flat as I've never seen it before or since on that coast, and the light went round over it, and in the stillness I smelled, very faintly, very close, something that might have been lavender.

It lasted perhaps a minute.

Then the wind came back, and I went down the stairs and locked the door behind me and drove back to Penmorran in the dark.

---

The holiday lets at Carrow Point opened the following Easter. I've looked at the reviews. I'm not proud of this, but I have. Most of them are what you'd expect — stunning location, bit remote, water pressure could be better, bring your own wine. But there's a pattern in them, if you know to look. I keep a list.

*"Strangely peaceful."*

*"Best sleep I've had in years — something about the back bedroom."*

*"Woke up and someone had put the kettle on. Assumed it was my husband but he swears it wasn't!"*

*"Found a little white pebble on the doorstep the morning we left. Kept it as a souvenir. Hope that's allowed."*

That last one was from a woman travelling alone. She gave the place five stars. She wrote, at the end of her review, *I needed this more than I knew.*

I think about that a lot.

---

There's a thing people say about lighthouses, which is that the light isn't for the keeper. The keeper never sees the light, not really, not the way the ships do — he's inside it, behind it, tending it, and from inside, the light is just a lamp, just a wick that needs trimming and a lens that needs cleaning and a log that needs filling in. It's the ships that see the light. It's the ships that are saved by it. The keeper just keeps.

I used to think that was a sad thing. Now I'm not sure.

Samuel Hosking kept a light for thirty-one years. He also kept someone company who had no other company. He kept a book. He kept his word. *I would never*, she said, and she never did — I looked it up; not one of the dozen assistant keepers who served under him at Carrow came to any harm, not a fall, not a drowning, not so much as a broken finger. Polglase, the last of them, lived to ninety and told his grandchildren that Carrow was "the kindest station on the coast," which, if you know anything about the service, is not a phrase that gets used about lighthouses.

Kept. That was the word on the paper. Kept.

I've started, in a small way, to keep things myself. I don't mean that mystically. I mean — I've started keeping a book. Not for work. My own. I bought it in Penmorran for considerably more than one and six. I write the weather in it. I write what I found that day in whatever old house I was crawling through, the things that don't go in the report: a child's name scratched into a window frame, a love letter behind a fireplace, a ration book, a tooth. I write when I'm lonely, which is less often than I'd have guessed, and when I'm happy, which is more.

Kit says I'm turning into a lighthouse keeper.

I tell him there are worse things to turn into.

---

And sometimes, when I'm working late in a building that's been empty a long time, I find myself saying, before I start, out loud and feeling only a little silly about it: "Hello. I'm Ilse. I'm just here to look. I'll be careful with everything."

Be civil, Davies said.

It costs nothing. And you never know who's listening, in the old places, who's been waiting a long time for someone to come and say their name.

---

## Part Two: The Other Book

I thought that was the end of it. I want to say that clearly, because what came next came as a surprise, and I don't want anyone thinking I went looking for it.

About eighteen months after I put the tin back under the floor at Carrow, I got a call from Priya Venkataraman. It was a Tuesday. I was in Bodmin, measuring a Methodist chapel that was going to become, of all things, a climbing wall.

"You remember the Carrow ledger," she said. Not a question.

"I remember."

"Someone's brought me another one."

---

It had come in with a bequest — the whole contents of a house in Falmouth belonging to a man named Edwin Pengelly, who had died at eighty-seven with no surviving family and had left everything to the county records office "for the use of anyone who wants to know." His solicitor had been bemused by this. Priya had been less bemused, because she'd spent twenty years receiving the boxed-up remnants of people's lives, and she knew that some people, at the end, just want someone to know.

Pengelly. I felt the name land in my chest before my mind caught up with why.

"The boatman's family," I said.

"Great-grandson, near as I can tell. The boat stayed in the family three generations. Edwin was the last one to run it — took tourists out round the point in the seventies, before he retired." She paused. "Ilse, there's a logbook. The boat's logbook. The original one. From the 1800s."

"And?"

"And I think you need to come and read it yourself."

---

The Pengelly logbook was a different creature from Hosking's ledger. It was a working document, a boatman's book, the kind of thing nobody writes for posterity — dates, tides, passengers, cargo, fares. *Paraffin 4 drums Carrow. Flour 2 sacks. Mr Davies 1 letter.* The handwriting was blunt and uneven, the spelling inventive. Old Pengelly had not been a man of letters.

Priya had marked a page with a strip of acid-free card.

The entry was from the spring of the year that both books had worked so hard to obscure. The year had been scratched out here too — not by Pengelly, Priya thought, judging by the different ink, but by someone later. Someone who had gone back.

The entry read:

> *Thursday. Tide 11.40. To Carrow — stores, 1 passenger. Mrs Davies. She said Tom expected her. Landed her at the steps 12.20 and she went up. Fine day.*

And then, below it, in the same blunt hand but pressed so hard the nib had scored the paper:

> *I did not tell her.*

That was all. *I did not tell her.*

"Tell her what?" I said.

Priya turned the page. Then another. Then several more — weather, tides, paraffin, flour — until she came to a second marker.

This one was not a log entry. It was a letter, folded small, tucked between the pages, written on a sheet torn from the back of the same book. Pengelly's handwriting again, but slower, more careful, as though he'd taken a long time over it.

---

> *To whoever has this book after me.*
>
> *I am a plain man and I do not write easy so I will be short.*
>
> *I took Mary Davies out to Carrow in the spring. She had a letter from Tom saying come. I did not tell her what I knew, which was that Tom had wrote to the Board two weeks before asking to be moved to another station, any station, as far as could be. I had carried the letter myself. I knew because he asked me to read it over for him, him being no great hand with a pen either, and he wanted it right.*
>
> *He did not want her out there. I think he was frightened of what the Board would do. Or I think he was frightened of something else. I do not know. But he had wrote to her to come before he lost his nerve and then wrote to the Board after, and he never wrote to her again to say stop, and I did not tell her when I had the chance in my boat with the wind fair and her face so glad.*
>
> *I landed her and she went up the steps and I never saw her again.*
>
> *When I came out the next week with the stores Tom met me at the landing alone. I asked after her and he said she had gone back on Trevail's boat Monday. Trevail does not run to Carrow. I said nothing. God forgive me I said nothing.*
>
> *I do not know what happened on that rock. I will never know. But I know that she went up those steps happy and I could have stopped her and did not. I have carried that.*
>
> *If anyone reads this and finds her, tell her Pengelly is sorry. Tell her I should have said.*
>
> *J. Pengelly*

---

I read it three times. Priya, very kindly, went to make tea and left me alone with it.

It changed things. Not the facts, exactly — Hosking's ledger had already told me Mary came and never left — but the shape of the facts. Hosking had believed, or chosen to believe, that Davies loved her, that he'd asked for her, that whatever happened to her was some sad accident and that Davies had kept the light and her secret together out of grief. *I do not blame him.* That's what he wrote.

But Davies had tried to run. Davies had written to the Board asking to be sent away, anywhere, as far as could be, two weeks before she arrived. And when she arrived anyway — when she came up the steps glad, with seven white stones in her pocket — something happened. And he lied about it. And then he kept the light alone for however many months or years until the January gale when he went up on the gallery and laughed and stepped off.

*I think she called him and he went*, Hosking wrote.

Maybe she did. But I sat in Priya's conservation room in Truro with the fluorescent lights buzzing and I thought: what if she didn't call him for love? What if she called him because he owed her?

And then I thought about the voice on the gallery, close enough to feel on the skin. *I would never.*

*Never*, she said. Never what? Never hurt Jago? Never do to Hosking's young assistant what had been done to her?

Or never do what she'd done to Davies?

---

Priya came back with the tea. She looked at my face and set the mug down very carefully, the way you'd set something down near an animal that might bolt.

"It's a lot," she said.

"I don't know what it means."

"Maybe it doesn't mean anything in particular. Maybe it's just — a man who felt guilty. People write things like this all the time. I've got a whole box of deathbed confessions in the basement. Most of them are about stealing sheep."

"He says 'if anyone finds her.' *If anyone finds her.* As though she's still there to be found."

Priya didn't say anything to that. After a minute she said, "There's one more thing. It's not in the logbook. It was in the box with it."

She brought out a small envelope, very old, unsealed. Inside was a photograph.

It was the same photograph — or nearly. A woman standing in the doorway of the keeper's cottage at Carrow, the cracked step at her feet. I'd seen Hosking's description of it; I'd never seen the photograph itself, because it wasn't in the tin. Hosking had put it back in Davies's sea chest, and the sea chest had gone wherever the Board sent dead men's things.

But this was a second print. A copy. And on the back, in Pengelly's blunt handwriting:

*Mrs Davies at Carrow. Tom gave me this to keep when he was courting, to show her mother he was serious. I never gave it back.*

I turned it over again and looked at her face for the first time.

She was young — younger than I'd pictured her. Twenty-five, maybe. Dark hair pinned up, a few strands escaping. A plain dress. She wasn't smiling in the stiff way people did for photographs then; she was smiling as though someone just out of frame had said something funny. One hand rested on the door frame. The other was closed, loosely, at her side, as though she was holding something small.

A pebble, I thought. Of course.

---

## Part Three: Finding

I'm not going to pretend I behaved entirely rationally over the next few months. I'm a surveyor. My job is to determine the condition of things. And I'd been handed a building — two books, a photograph, a grave — that had a defect in it somewhere, a hidden failure, and I couldn't leave it alone any more than I could leave a soft spot in a floor.

Where was Mary?

Not in the churchyard. The stone in Penmorran says *And Mary his wife, who waited*, but I checked the burial register — Priya helped — and there's only one burial recorded under that stone. Thomas. Mary's name was added to the inscription later, by whom nobody knows, and her body was never in the ground there. Whoever put her name on the stone either didn't know where she was or knew and couldn't say.

Not in the Truro records, either. She never went back to Truro. Her mother-in-law — the woman Mary had been fleeing, "looking at me that way" — died a few years later, and her will left everything to "my son Thomas, and should he predecease me, to the Wesleyan chapel." No mention of a daughter-in-law at all, living or dead. As though Mary had simply been erased.

So: she came out to Carrow, and she didn't leave.

I went back to the Trinity House archives, the bits that weren't digitised, and this time I made the trip to London. Two days in a reading room with the radiators clanking and a very patient archivist named Mr. Adeyemi bringing me box after box of station correspondence.

I found Tom Davies's letter to the Board. Pengelly's account was accurate — a short, stiff request for transfer, "for reasons of a personal nature which I would prefer not to set down." The Board's reply, a fortnight later, was a refusal. Carrow was short-handed; no transfer could be considered before the autumn.

The Board's refusal would have arrived on Pengelly's boat. The same boat, I realised, checking the dates against the logbook, that carried Mary.

She arrived on the rock with the letter that trapped him there.

---

And then — this was late on the second day, my eyes aching, Mr. Adeyemi starting to make meaningful noises about closing time — I found one more thing. A report from the district superintendent, filed the following summer, regarding "alterations at Carrow Point."

> *The Principal Keeper, Davies, has without authority undertaken works to the base of the tower on the landward side, consisting of the laying of a new section of flagstone floor in the oil store and the building up of the wall adjoining. He states this was necessary owing to damp. I have inspected the work and find it competently done though irregular. I have admonished him for undertaking structural works without the Board's sanction but do not propose further action, the work being sound.*

I read it, and then I read it again, and then I sat back in the hard reading room chair and closed my eyes.

The oil store.

*I buried it in the rocks below the oil store*, Hosking wrote, on the very first page, about the gull. *Which I suppose is foolish.*

He'd been standing right there. Thirty-one years, and every time he went for paraffin he walked across that floor.

---

I want to be careful here, because this is the point in the story where I have to talk about things I did that I'm not entirely proud of, and things I didn't do that I'm not sure about either.

What I did not do was go to Carrow with a crowbar. I want that clear.

What I did was write a report. A proper one, to the heritage trust, drawing on the superintendent's account of "irregular" structural alterations, recommending a ground-penetrating radar survey of the oil store floor "to assess the condition of sub-floor structures and any voids which may affect the integrity of the tower base." All of which was, technically, a legitimate concern. Unauthorised Victorian structural work is exactly the kind of thing you want to know about in a building you're renting to tourists.

The trust agreed. The survey was done in March, nearly two years after I first lifted the floorboard in the back bedroom. I was there.

The radar showed a void beneath the flagstones in the northeast corner of the oil store. About the size you'd expect.

---

What happened after that went through proper channels. The coroner was informed. An archaeologist from the county came. The holiday lets were closed for three weeks, and the trust put out a carefully worded statement about "historic human remains discovered during routine structural assessment," and the local paper ran a story with a photo of the lighthouse at sunset and the headline *SECRET OF CARROW POINT*, which made me wince but which I suppose was fair.

They lifted the flags on a grey, still morning. I wasn't allowed close — I wasn't anything, officially, just the surveyor who wrote the report — but the archaeologist, a brisk woman named Dr. Halloran who had clearly decided early on that I knew more than I was saying and had decided not to push, let me stand in the doorway.

She was there. Small, curled on her side, wrapped in what had been a blanket. There was not much left. There was enough.

In the bones of her right hand, Dr. Halloran told me afterward, they found seven small white quartz pebbles.

She'd held on to them. Whatever happened — and the coroner was never able to say what happened; there were no injuries the bones could show, which means only that whatever killed her didn't leave a mark on bone — whatever happened, she'd held on.

---

I don't know what happened on that rock. Pengelly didn't know. Hosking didn't know, or didn't want to. I've constructed a dozen versions in my head and I don't trust any of them. Maybe Tom Davies, cornered by the Board's refusal and terrified of what discovery would cost him, did something unforgivable. Maybe Mary fell ill in that damp back bedroom — there were fevers, then, that took a young woman in three days — and Tom, panicked, alone, with no way to explain her presence or her death without losing everything, put her where nobody would find her, and then spent every remaining day of his life walking over her to fetch the paraffin. Maybe it was something else entirely.

I can't know. That's the honest answer, and I've learned, from these two books, to value the honest answer.

What I know is this: she went up the steps glad. She held on to the stones. And something of her stayed — stayed angry, maybe, for a while, long enough to call one man up onto a gallery in a January gale — but then stayed for thirty-one years after that and laid the table and hummed "The White Rose" and put a cool hand on a lonely man's forehead in the winter of the big freeze.

People can change, Kit says, when I tell him this. Maybe the dead can too.

---

## Part Four: The Burial

Mary Davies was buried in the churchyard at Penmorran in late May, in a small ceremony that was organised, in the end, mostly by Mrs. Ogunleye, who said that if the poor woman had waited this long she deserved a proper send-off and not some council job.

The vicar — a young woman, newly ordained, who'd been rather thrilled to be asked — read the service. The village turned out, more of them than I'd expected; this is the kind of story that small places hold on to. Priya came down from Truro. Dr. Halloran came, in a black coat, looking slightly uncomfortable. Kit drove down from Leeds and stood beside me in a borrowed tie.

There was a question, beforehand, about where to put her. The obvious place was with Tom, under the stone that already bore her name — *And Mary his wife, who waited.* And there was a part of me that recoiled from that, given what I suspected, given Pengelly's *I did not tell her.*

But it wasn't my decision. In the end the vicar found, in the old parish records, a note that had been written in the margin of the burial register beside Tom Davies's entry, decades after his death, in a hand that I recognised before Priya confirmed it. A tall, careful, old man's copperplate, going shaky.

> *His wife Mary lies elsewhere. When she is found, do not lay her here. Lay her by the wall facing the sea, where she can see the light. S.H.*

He knew. Or he guessed. He'd known enough, at least, to leave instructions.

So they laid her by the wall, facing the sea. And from that spot, if you stand there at dusk — I have — you can see the Carrow light come round, every fifteen seconds, steady, out across the bay.

---

There was one more grave I visited that day.

Samuel Hosking is buried at the far end of the churchyard, in a plain plot with a plain stone that says only his name, his dates, and *Keeper of the Carrow Light, 31 years.* Nobody had tended it in a long time. It was overgrown with ivy and the lettering was half lost under lichen.

After the service, when everyone else had gone down to the Ship for sandwiches and the kind of drinking that follows funerals in Cornish villages, I went back up with a pair of secateurs I'd borrowed from Mrs. Ogunleye and a stiff brush, and I cleared it. It took about an hour. Kit sat on a bench nearby and didn't help and didn't need to.

When it was clean, I took something out of my coat pocket.

Thirty-one white pebbles. Hosking had carried them ashore in his coat — *I have them in my coat pocket as I write this* — and I'd always wondered what became of them. Ruth Hosking had them, it turned out. They'd come down to her through the family in a twist of paper labelled, in Samuel's hand, *Hers. Do not throw away.* She'd given them to me, the last time I saw her, three weeks before she died. She said, "You'll know what to do with them."

I hadn't, until that afternoon.

I laid them on his grave in a straight row. Very straight. One for each year.

And then — I'd thought about this for a long time, and I want to be clear that I know it's sentimental and I did it anyway — I took one pebble back. Just one. I walked across the churchyard to the new grave by the wall, the raw earth still dark, the flowers from the service still bright, and I set it on top.

"So you've got one each," I said, out loud, to nobody. "You can share. He'd want you to have it."

Kit, on his bench, very kindly pretended not to have heard.

---

We drove out to Carrow that evening, Kit and I, because he'd never seen it and I wanted him to. The holiday lets were reopening the following week; the trust had given me a key "for any final inspection," which was a polite fiction everybody understood.

We climbed the tower. Kit, who doesn't like heights, went very pale and gripped the rail and said, "Christ, Ilse," and then, after a minute, more quietly, "Oh. *Oh.*"

Because from up there, the whole world is sea. The bay curves away on one side towards Penmorran's scatter of lights, and on the other there's nothing at all, just water going out grey and then silver and then dark to the edge of everything. And behind you the great lens, and inside it the small bright light turning.

We stood there while the dusk came on. The lamp lit itself. It went round.

I didn't say anything this time. I didn't feel I needed to. Kit, beside me, was quiet in the way he gets quiet in churches.

The wind was from the west, force 3 or so. It didn't drop. The sea didn't go flat. There was no lavender.

And I found I was glad of that, in a way I can't completely explain. As though the stillness — the dead calm, the voice by my ear — had been something she needed, once, to make herself known, and didn't need now. As though she'd been found, and could stop counting.

The light went round. Every fifteen seconds. Steady.

"It's beautiful," Kit said eventually.

"Yes."

"Are you going to write this down? All of it?"

"I already have," I said. "I've been writing it the whole time."

---

## Part Five: What the Keeper Keeps

That was four years ago now.

I'm still a surveyor. I still crawl around in old buildings with a moisture meter and a torch, and I still find things — not often, but sometimes. A child's shoe in a wall cavity, put there to keep off bad luck. A bundle of letters in a biscuit tin under a stair. A name carved into a beam by a carpenter in 1740, with a tiny drawing of a heart beside it. I photograph them. I write them in my book. Usually I leave them where they are.

People ask me, when I tell this story — and I've told it, now, more times than I can count, at dinner parties and in pubs and once, memorably, to a very drunk man on a delayed train out of Exeter who turned out to be a retired Trinity House engineer and who cried — people ask me whether I believe it. Whether I really think there was a ghost at Carrow.

And I've thought about how to answer that honestly, because honesty is the thing these two books taught me most.

Here is my honest answer.

I know that a woman died on that rock and was hidden, and that her husband lied, and that a boatman carried the guilt of not warning her for the rest of his life. Those are facts. They're documented. I can show you the paper.

I know that a man named Samuel Hosking stayed at a remote and lonely station for thirty-one years, turning down promotion twice, and that he wrote in his private book that he was not unhappy, that he was keeping someone company. I know he left instructions about her burial decades before anyone found her. I know he gathered up thirty-one white pebbles from a step and carried them ashore and labelled them *Hers*. Those are facts too.

I know that the holiday guests at Carrow Point write, more often than you'd expect, about the strange peace of the back bedroom. I have a list.

I know that I stood on a gallery at dusk and the wind dropped and the sea went flat and I smelled lavender. That's a fact as well, in the sense that it happened to me. What it *means* is another question, and I'm not sure I'm the right person to answer it.

What I believe — and this is belief, not fact; I'm keeping them separate, the way Hosking kept the Board's blue book separate from his own green one — what I believe is that people leave things behind them. Sometimes those things are objects. Sometimes they're stories. Sometimes they're a kind of — pressure, I suppose. A shape in the air of a place where something mattered very much. Whether that's a ghost, or grief, or just the long echo of attention that a place absorbs when someone lives in it carefully for thirty-one years — I don't know. I'm not sure the distinction is as important as people think.

What I believe is that kindness can outlast the person who offers it. And that civility, offered to something you don't understand, can turn over time into something much larger.

Be civil, Davies said. It was the only good advice he ever gave, and he didn't follow it himself.

Hosking followed it. Hosking followed it for thirty-one years. And at the end of his book he wrote: *It is more than a great many men get. I know that now.*

---

I've got my own book on the desk beside me as I write this. Green cloth, as it happens; I went looking for one deliberately. It's nearly full. I'll start another soon.

Tonight the weather is: wind south-west, force 5, rain coming in from the Atlantic. Barometer falling. I'm not anywhere near a lighthouse — I'm in a rented flat in Exeter with a radiator that knocks and a neighbour who plays the cello badly and with great feeling every evening at seven. But I write the weather anyway. It's a habit now. It keeps me honest, somehow, to start with the plain facts before I get to the rest.

And then I write the rest.

Today I surveyed a farmhouse near Crediton that's been in the same family for two hundred years and is about to be sold to people who are going to knock most of it down. In the dairy, behind a loose stone in the wall, I found a small glass bottle, corked, with a folded piece of paper inside. A witch bottle, probably — they put them in walls to trap bad luck. But when I held it up to the light, the paper inside didn't look like a charm. It looked like a letter.

I didn't open it. I put it back.

But I said, first, out loud, standing in that cold dairy with the rain starting: "Hello. I'm Ilse. I found your letter. I'm going to leave it where it is, because it's yours. But I'll make sure someone knows it's here, so it doesn't get lost when they take the wall down."

And then — I'll tell you this, and you can make of it what you like — I stood there a moment longer than I needed to. Just in case. Just to be civil.

The rain kept on. The wind didn't drop. Nothing happened at all.

Which is fine. Most of the time, nothing does. Most of the time the past is weather and stores and the occasional gull against the glass, and you write it down and go on.

But every so often — once in a season, sometimes less — the table is laid when you come down from the watch. And you sit, and you eat, and you say thank you.

And the light goes round.

---

## Coda: An Entry

I'll end with an entry from my own book, written last autumn, on the anniversary of the day Samuel Hosking went ashore for good. I drove down to Penmorran for it. I'm not sure why. It felt like the sort of thing you mark.

---

**4 October.** Wind W, force 3. Clear and bright, cold for the season. Sunrise 07:24, near enough to what he wrote that it made me catch my breath.

Went to the churchyard first. Both graves tended — not by me. Someone's been keeping them. Fresh flowers on Mary's, Michaelmas daisies, purple. Hosking's had been weeded. Mrs. Ogunleye, I'd guess, or the young vicar, or one of the holiday guests who reads the little framed account the trust put up in the cottage hallway. (I wrote it. They asked. I kept it short.)

The pebbles were still on Hosking's grave. Thirty of them, in a row. Somebody's straightened them.

On Mary's grave, by the flowers, there was the one I'd moved. And beside it, another.

I didn't put it there. I asked Mrs. Ogunleye; she didn't either. A white quartz pebble, round, smooth, the kind you find at Porthallow and not here.

I don't know who left it. Somebody civil, I expect.

Drove out to Carrow after. Didn't go in — there were guests, a young couple, I saw them on the gallery waving at a seal. Sat on the rocks below the tower instead, near where the oil store window looks out, and watched the sea for an hour. It was moving, ordinary, the way the sea moves, grey-green and restless, nothing remarkable about it at all.

Lamp lit itself at 18:47.

It went round.

I said goodnight, and I meant it for all three of them, and I drove home.

---

*Kept.*

---

## Afterword: On Keeping

I've been asked, since I first wrote this account down, what I think the story is *about*. People want stories to be about something; I understand that. I'm a person who measures things for a living, and there's a part of me that wants a final figure too, a number at the bottom of the column.

So here is my attempt, for what it's worth.

I think it's about the difference between keeping something and holding on to it. Tom Davies held on — to his position, to his secret, to his fear of what the Board would do — and the holding destroyed him and very nearly destroyed her memory along with him. Pengelly held on to his guilt for a lifetime and wrote it down at the end because he couldn't carry it any further. Even Mary, I think, held on for a while — held on to the seven stones in her closed hand, held on to whatever anger called a man up onto a gallery in a gale.

But Hosking *kept*. That's different. Keeping is active. It's trimming the wick and cleaning the lens and filling in the log, night after night, not because anything dramatic will happen but because it's the work and the work matters. It's laying a table for someone. It's saying a name into the wind and not being embarrassed. It's carrying thirty-one stones ashore and labelling them so they won't be thrown away. It's leaving a note in the margin of a burial register for whoever comes after you, decades later, so they'll know where to lay her down.

Holding on is about what you're afraid to lose. Keeping is about what you're willing to tend.

And I think — this is the part I'm least sure of, and so I'll say it last — I think that in thirty-one years of being kept, Mary changed. I think whatever was angry in her, whatever called Davies over the rail, was slowly tended into something else, the way a wild thing can be gentled by someone who's patient enough and doesn't ask too much. *I would never*, she said. And she kept her word, as Hosking kept his.

Two people on a rock, one living and one not, keeping each other company and keeping a light that neither of them would ever see the way the ships saw it.

It's more than a great many people get.

I know that now.

---

*Wind W, force 3. Lamp lit. All well.*

---

And because I said I wouldn't stop, and because there's always more weather, I'll keep going a little longer — not with Carrow, which has had its ending, but with the book itself, the green one on my desk, which doesn't end because I haven't.

---

**12 November.** Wind N, force 6. Sleet in the morning, clearing by noon. The cellist next door has moved on from Elgar to something I don't recognise and suspect he's composing himself. It is not good. It is very sincere.

Surveyed a terrace in Topsham for a housing association. Nothing found but damp and a 1970s *Jackie* magazine under the lino, a free gift still inside — a plastic ring with a pink stone. I put it on my little finger to see if it fit. It didn't. I put it back in the magazine and the magazine back under the lino and told the contractor to leave it when they relay the floor. He looked at me like I was mad. He'll leave it, though. They usually do, if you ask nicely.

Kit rang. He's seeing someone — a pharmacist called Ade who, Kit says, "doesn't believe in anything but is very nice about it." I said that sounded like a good balance. Kit said, "That's what you'd say," and I said, "Yes," and we both laughed.

**13 November.** Wind N, force 4. Bright, cold. Frost on the cars.

Letter came from the trust. The Carrow cottages had their best year since opening. They've had a request from a woman in Leeds — no relation to Kit, I checked — who wants to know whether she can book the back bedroom specifically, every year, for the first week of October. The trust didn't know what to tell her. They forwarded it to me, as though I'm some sort of authority.

I wrote back: *Let her have it.*

**15 November.** Wind SW, force 5. Rain.

Couldn't sleep. Got up at three and sat at the window with tea. The street was empty, orange under the sodium lights, rain slanting through them. I thought about Hosking coming down from the watch at 02:00 and finding the table laid.

Nobody's going to lay a table for me. I know that. I'm not maudlin about it. But I found myself, at half past three in the morning, getting a second cup down from the cupboard and setting it across the table from mine. Not for anyone in particular. Just — so it was there.

It felt foolish. I left it anyway.

In the morning it was still there, empty, exactly where I'd put it, which is of course what cups do. I washed it and put it away.

But I slept, afterwards. Properly. Better than I had in weeks.

**18 November.** Wind W, force 3. Fine.

A thing I've noticed: since I started keeping this book, I notice weather more. Not just the obvious — rain, wind — but the small things. The way light comes differently through a north window in November. The particular smell of the air before snow. The days when the sea, even here, ten miles inland, seems to make itself felt somehow, a kind of pressure change you register in your sinuses before your mind catches up.

Hosking would have known all of that by instinct after thirty-one years. Davies too, probably. Mary — maybe not; she was a town girl, from Truro. I wonder if she learned it, in all that time on the rock. I wonder if, by the end, she could feel a gale coming the way he could.

I like to think so. I like to think they'd sit on the gallery, the two of them, and she'd know before he did. And she'd hum something, to warn him, and he'd go in and check the barometer, and it would be falling.

**20 November.** Calm. Fog.

Fog all day. Couldn't see the end of the street. The whole city gone soft and grey and close.

On days like this at Carrow they'd run the fog signal — a great horn, compressed air, one long blast every thirty seconds. Hosking wrote about it: *A long morning of it.* Hours and hours of that sound going out over the water, for ships nobody could see.

I've been thinking about that. About doing something for hours, regularly, faithfully, for people you can't see and will never meet, who may not even be there.

That's most work, really. That's most kindness. You put the signal out into the fog and you trust that someone hears it.

Fog lifted at four. Sun came through red and low.

**22 November.** Wind SW, force 4.

Priya rang. Another bequest, another box. She says there's nothing in it like the Carrow books — "just a woman's recipe cards from the 1950s, about three hundred of them, annotated" — but she thought I'd like to know that she's started reading them properly instead of just cataloguing them. "Since Carrow," she said. "I read everything now. It takes ages. My manager's furious."

I asked what the annotations said.

"Mostly 'too much salt' or 'Frank liked this.' But there's one on a lemon cake that says 'made for Joan the day she told me. Didn't help but she ate two slices.'"

We were both quiet for a moment.

"I don't know who Joan is," Priya said. "Or what she told her. I'll never know."

"No."

"I'm keeping the card out, though. On my desk."

"Good," I said.

**25 November.** Wind W, force 5. Showers.

There's a habit people have, when they find out about Carrow, of asking me whether I've had "any more experiences." As though I'm a sort of medium now, or as though once you've been touched by one strange thing you become a magnet for them.

The honest answer is no. Not really. Nothing like Carrow. I've been in dozens of old buildings since, and some of them have felt sad and some have felt peaceful and one or two have felt, frankly, unpleasant, the way some rooms do, and I couldn't tell you whether any of that is anything more than damp and acoustics and my own imagination furnishing the place.

But I'm civil to all of them. Every one. I say hello and I say I'll be careful and I say goodbye when I leave.

And I've noticed something, which is that the people I work with — contractors, owners, estate agents, the occasional archaeologist — have started to do it too. Not all of them. Not even most. But some. I was on a job in Launceston last month with a roofer called Gary, a huge man with a neck tattoo of a Rottweiler, and as we went up into the attic I heard him say, under his breath, to the dark, "All right? Just us. Won't be long."

He saw me looking and went red to the ears.

"My nan used to do it," he said. "I forgot about it until you started."

That's how it spreads, I think. Not as belief. As habit. As manners.

**28 November.** Wind S, force 3. Mild.

Went down to Penmorran again. No reason. I just wanted to see the sea.

Mrs. Ogunleye gave me a proper tea, which was again a full roast dinner, and told me the village news. The young vicar is engaged to the man with the strimmer. Ruth Hosking's cottage has been bought by a family from Birmingham who've kept all the brass and polish it every Saturday "because it seemed rude not to." Someone has started leaving white pebbles on the steps of the old lifeboat station, and nobody knows who, and the harbourmaster has stopped sweeping them away.

"It's become a thing," Mrs. Ogunleye said, a bit ruefully. "You've made it a thing."

"I didn't mean to."

"No. Well." She refilled my tea. "There's worse things to be a thing."

After, I walked out along the cliff path as far as the point where you can see Carrow straight across the water. I stood there until it got dark. The light came on. It went round.

I counted. Fifteen seconds, every time. Steady as a heartbeat.

**1 December.** Wind NE, force 6. Bitter.

First proper cold of the winter. The cellist has stopped playing in the evenings; I think he's gone away for a while. I find I miss it, even the bad bits. Especially the bad bits. There was something brave about all that sincere wrongness coming through the wall every night at seven.

Thought today about the thirty-one pebbles on Hosking's grave — thirty, now, plus the one I moved, plus the one somebody else left. Thirty-two stones for two people. That seems about right. Not even, but right.

I've started a small collection of my own. Not white quartz — I'm not going to steal their symbol. Just ordinary stones, one from each building where I've found something worth keeping. A flint from the Crediton dairy. A bit of slate from the Topsham terrace. A pebble from the gutter outside the Methodist chapel in Bodmin that's now a climbing wall. They sit on my windowsill in a row.

Not very straight. I'm not as tidy as Hosking.

But I'm keeping count.

**3 December.** Calm. Clear. Very cold.

Clear night. From the flat I can't see stars, only the orange glow of the city, but I went out at midnight and walked up to the park on the hill where the light pollution's a bit thinner and I could make out Orion, and the Plough, and a few others I don't know the names of.

Sailors steered by those, once. Before lighthouses, and alongside them. Lights put up there by nobody, keeping nobody company, going round and round on their own slow schedule.

I stood in the cold and said hello to them too. It seemed only civil.

---

And that's where I'll stop for now — not because the book's finished, because it isn't, and not because there's nothing more to say, because there's always the weather. But because a keeper's log isn't meant to be read all at once. It's meant to be lived a day at a time, one entry and then the next, lamp lit and lamp extinguished, all the long ordinary nights between the rare ones when the table is laid.

Tomorrow I'll write the weather. And then I'll write whatever else there is.

Wind NE, force 2, falling light.

Lamp lit.

All well.
